items.title: At least 11 dead, 34 injured after ‘vile’ attack on Ukraine on Putin’s birthday, Zelenskyy says – Europe live
items.author: Jakub Krupa
items.content:
Ukraine president confirms series of attacks on Pryluky, Dnipro, Kremenchik, Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv

The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen condemned the latest round of Russian attacks on Ukraine, blaming Moscow for “pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror.”

“Russia is pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror. Trying to make daily life impossible for Ukrainians who want to live in peace.

To protect people and infrastructure, Europe is stepping up. Others must step up their support too.”

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched “one fo the most vile strikes” on Ukraine last night, targeting the country’s energy infrastructure overnight.

At least 11 people were killed , and more than 34 injured in a series of attacks on Pryluky, Dnipro, Kremenchik, Zaporizhzhia, and Kyiv, which Zelenskyy ironically called “a birthday gift for Putin” who turns 74 today.

“ Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity. That is why every day we are looking for missiles for Patriot systems that can and must actually protect people’s lives here, in Ukrainian skies,” Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha went further, saying:

“ On Putin’s birthday, Russian generals brought him his favorite present: war crimes. ”

“What Russian generals fail to tell Putin is that he is not winning this war and never will. …

I urge all partners to give Putin real presents that will help him finally choose diplomacy over war. Stronger sanctions on his military-industrial complex, including facilities producing ballistic missiles and the Rassvet satellite system, as well as stronger support for Ukraine, including all kinds of air defence and energy assistance ahead of winter.

But his ultimate present will be a dock in The Hague. We are preparing the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine for practical launch already next year. Putin and his friends should know that accountability is inevitable.”

Elsewhere, I will bring you the latest from France , as high school protests continue after a major march in Paris, which ended with sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, and officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.

Following allegations of police brutality, interior minister Laurent Nuñez suspended the use of stun grenades at the protests, after a 15-year-old reportedly lost a hand on Monday, and a 14-year old lost several teeth.

The French PM, Sébastien Lecornu, is expected to speak later today to set out his plans for responding to the protests.

I will bring you also all other news from across Europe .

It’s Wednesday, 7 October 2026 , it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live .

items.lbText:
Minister says use of grenades has been stopped ‘until we know what happened’ as protests across France continue

How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

France is suspending the use of stun grenades by police at high-school demonstrations, the interior minister has said, amid mounting accusations of police brutality during a fortnight of protests marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds.

Laurent Nuñez told RTL radio on Wednesday that he had ordered a temporary halt to the use of the grenades “in the context of the high-school students’ movement” after a 15-year-old lost a hand during a protest in Lens, northern Fance, on Monday.

Authorities have not confirmed the exact circumstances – in particular, whether the boy had picked the grenade up or had been struck by it – but said up to 200 protesters had been hurling projectiles at police when the riot squad intervened.

Nuñez said he was suspending use of the grenades “until we know exactly what happened”.

The boy’s mother said on Wednesday that her son’s hand had been amputated. She told BFMTV: “His life has been stolen. He’s a 15-year-old kid, how can children be treated like that?” She said her son had not tried to pick the grenade up.

At least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff have been injured since the start of the protests over chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days . About 750 police offers have also been wounded.

Nuñez said 18 internal police investigations have been launched over allegations of brutality during the demonstrations, including one incident in which a young protester lost multiple teeth and another in which a student lost the use of an eye.

He said inquiries were always opened over accusations of “non-proportional” policing, but insisted officers were there to protect the students. Rights groups and trades unions have repeatedly accused the police of using unnecessary force.

The decision came a day after at least 250,000 pupils, parents, teachers and unionists took to the streets in cities across France on the biggest day yet of the campaign, prompting the president, Emmanuel Macron, to hold an emergency cabinet meeting.

Most marches passed off without serious incident, but some – including in Paris – ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, is due to make a speech on Wednesday on the demonstrations as well as the dire state of the country’s finances, which is severely constraining the government’s capacity to act on the protesters’ demands.

Lecornu on Tuesday condemned the violence and told parliament it could not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against the protesters.

Over the past fortnight demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded with batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.

Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked, while more than 6,500 people have ​been arrested, almost all of them minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, nearly 1,500 of them under 18, the justice ministry has said.

Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France , said earlier this week that images and testimony from the protests “raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques”.

The education ministry said classes had been wholly or partially suspended in 528 of the country’s 3,700 lycées – high schools attended by pupils aged between 15 and 18 – on Wednesday, a significantly lower number than on Tuesday.

The protests, months before key presidential elections to choose Macron’s successor, have rattled a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s ​sky-high debt and weak economic growth.

They have also sparked a heated political row, with the government accusing the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades.

The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests, while urging non-violence.

items.lbText:
Record prices caused by global shortages amid shutdown of war-damaged refineries in Middle East and Russia

Shell’s refineries are expected to make almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel produced owing to record prices caused by shortages around the world.

In a market trading update on Wednesday, the energy supermajor forecast profit margins of $42 a barrel in the July to September period, far above the $24 a barrel of the second quarter and the previous high of about $28 in mid-2022.

The margins reflect the steep increase in the price of refined fuels, including diesel, relative to the cost of crude oil, as the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia squeezes supplies.

The Middle East crisis helped Europe’s biggest oil and gas company to a profit of almost $10bn (£7.5bn) for the second quarter of 2026, more than double the figure for the same period last year and its second highest quarterly earnings on record.

The market value of Shell, now the second largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index, climbed to a record high of £36.23 a share at the end of last month.

That share price was reached despite oil prices retreating from their 2026 peak of above $115 a barrel in spring to about $100. It was lifted by European gas prices, which doubled from the previous year over the summer, and record high diesel prices .

Global oil prices were slightly lower in the third quarter of the year. Brent crude averaged $85.60 a barrel, compared with $97.05 in the second quarter, but still well above the $68.14 recorded in the third quarter last year.

The diesel price premium over the global oil benchmark jumped above $100 a barrel for the first time, indicating record high profits from refining crude into fuels.

Shell operates some of Europe’s largest refineries alongside the French energy company TotalEnergies, which has the continent’s largest refining capacity.

TotalEnergies’ chief executive, Patrick Pouyanné, welcomed the opportunities created by the global energy crisis.

He told an industry conference in London this week: “We’re doing really well by being integrated. Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.”

Europe’s benchmark gas price index more than doubled to €70.50 (£60) in August. The price of gas reached an average of more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter before leaping to almost €64/MWh in the third quarter.

Shell’s gas production has been hard-hit by the Iran crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf, cutting its prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌per day (BOED) by a third.

Shell said on Wednesday that it expects gas production to climb to about 740,000 to 780,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌per day, ‌up sharply from its previous forecast of 570,000 to 630,000 BOED for the quarter. It produced about 631,000 BOED in the second quarter.

items.lbText:
Lawyers launch super-complaint after research shows officers frequently dismiss image-based abuse

Police forces are routinely failing to investigate complaints about the circulation of image-based abuse, previously known as “revenge pornography”, according to research that has triggered a super-complaint over the way such crimes are handled.

Lawyers have gathered evidence from 100 people who reported intimate images being shared online without their consent. Their research suggests that image-based abuse is still frequently dismissed or not recognised as criminal offending, despite being described by the former prime minister Keir Starmer as a national emergency.

Referrals to the Revenge Porn helpline, the charity that helps victims get non-consensual images removed from the internet, increased by more than 4,000% between 2015 and 2025, but data from 39 police forces in England and Wales shows that charges were lodged against perpetrators in an average of just 4.5% of cases last year. In some forces the figure was lower than 1%.

Some police officers responded inappropriately when women tried to register complaints, researchers found. One reported that the officer “almost giggled on the phone to me”, while another said the officer responded: “Boys will be boys.” Another said: “I bet you’ve learned your lesson.”

Image-based abuse overwhelmingly affects women and girls, who make up 98.9% of reported images.

Lawyers from Leigh Day and the charity the Centre for Women’s Justice are working with the charity #NotYourPorn to highlight systemic police failings in responding to image-based abuse, defined as “the taking, sharing or creating of intimate content without the survivor’s consent, or threatening to do so”.

They note that rapid innovations in AI are helping abusers find new ways to create and disseminate synthetic explicit material, sometimes known as deepfake content.

Their research classifies the policing response as “fragmented, inconsistent and incapable of meeting the scale of the threat posed by image-based abuse”. “Despite the increased public awareness, and the creation of new criminal offences designed to address this conduct, there has been no corresponding increase in charging rates, prosecutions or convictions,” the complaint says.

“The unavoidable conclusion is that the overwhelming majority of this offending goes unaddressed.”

Home Office data shows that there were only 569 charges issued for image-based abuse in 2025/2026. The Revenge Porn Helpline received almost 25,000 reports in 2025.

Researchers found that the vast majority of survivors of image-based abuse did not report it to the police, noting that “embarrassment, shame and fear” contributed to their reluctance. Police outsourced the evidence-gathering process to survivors in many cases, the report notes, leaving them to work out how to collate proof that the images were being disseminated widely and how to get the content removed from the internet.

“It felt like to them it wasn’t a priority, it wasn’t even a crime,” one woman told researchers. Another said: “Police involvement has not alleviated the harm caused by this offence. Instead, it has intensified my distress and left me feeling powerless and completely unsupported as a victim.”

A police super-complaint is a mechanism introduced in 2018 to allow concerns to be raised about ways in which the police operate that may significantly harm the interests of the public generally, rather than focusing on an individual force of officer.

The complaint will be jointly considered by the College of Policing and the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which will decide whether to respond by opening a wider investigation.

Harriet Bland, a lawyer with the Centre for Women’s Justice, said: “Without an urgent overhaul of police guidance and training on image-based abuse – which must be regularly updated – and a clear national strategy rolled out across forces, survivors will continue to be let down.”

items.lbText:
Average cost of home in September was £298,441, says Lloyds – about the same as year earlier and in August

UK house prices flatlined in September, according to a leading index, as rising mortgage costs started to weigh on the market.

The average cost of a home was £298,441, roughly the same as it was a year earlier and in the previous month, according to the tracker from Lloyds previously known as the Halifax HPI.

Economists polled by Reuters had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices, according to the median forecast, as well as a 0.2% annual increase.

It came after house prices fell by 0.3% in August , the first decline in three years, as prospective buyers were hit by geopolitical uncertainty, combined with higher mortgage rates and stretched affordability.

In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put prices up as a result of turmoil in the global bond markets, even though there has not been a change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year.

Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of base rate.”

On Monday the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 6% for the first time in three years . Rising mortgage rates are bad news for borrowers whose fixed-rate deals are ending, as well as prospective buyers who are hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a home and the sellers who want the best price from them.

It also adds to the squeeze facing consumers as a result of higher energy bills , linked to the Iran war, while rising prices elsewhere are raising concerns of a new cost of living crisis .

Asaam said: “While higher mortgage rates and wider economic uncertainty are encouraging some people to take a more measured approach, new inquiries from prospective buyers are now at their highest since February.”

He added that any movement in house prices was likely to remain modest.

Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at the estate agent Knight Frank, said: “This year has been a story of rising energy prices and stalling house prices, as the unpredictable Middle East conflict unfolds and drives borrowing costs higher. This month’s budget adds to the uncertainty as buyers and sellers wonder which of the recurring tax rumours proves to be true.”

The number of people applying for a mortgage to buy a property fell between July and September, as higher borrowing costs continued to affect prospective housebuyers’ budgets, according to quarterly figures from Stonebridge, one of the UK’s largest independent mortgage and protection networks.

Mortgage applications for home purchases fell by 18.2% in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, Stonebridge found, while applications from first-time buyers slumped 18.6% over the same period.

However, rising numbers of applications for remortgaging helped to slow the decline in overall mortgage activity.

items.lbText:
Models walk runway at the Louvre with flying cars hovering above as designer envisions city life in a warming world

In silk slip dresses, breezy vented tunics and gossamer layers of chiffon, the models on Louis Vuitton’s catwalk were perfectly dressed for an unseasonably warm October evening in Paris. As the show began at sunset it was still 24C.

This summer’s record temperatures were on designer Nicolas Ghesquiière’s mind. “The world is getting warmer, this definitely had a strong influence” he said.

The show was staged in an inner courtyard of the Louvre, the catwalk illuminated by the tail lights of a fleet of 34 flying cars in Vuitton’s signature Damier check raised on stilts above the catwalk.

The contrast between the futuristic set and the historic buildings was an elegant echo of the centrepiece of the Louvre, where IM Pei’s glass pyramid stands amid the French classical architecture.

The future is always on Ghesquière’s mind – his science fiction bent showed up in the models’ beaded silver fringes that were somewhere between space-age hair extensions and sun visors – and this season, he was thinking about life in the cities of the future, his models as pedestrians among flying cars. “I was thinking about a woman walking through traffic, and how in the urban environment we sometimes feel vulnerable and sometimes feel strong.”

The featherlight fabrics and free-floating silhouettes were a departure from the angular, ornate looks which are his signature. “I am a specialist in a kind of fashion that is like armour, fashion with strong architecture, but this summer I think we all felt like we needed a different wardrobe. The world is getting warmer. We need to think differently, for clothes to be relevant today and in the future.”

Zendaya wore a ruffled organza jacket last seen on her Odyssey press tour and the Rivals actor Bella Maclean was in sleek black tailoring. Ghesquière took his bow casually dressed in jeans – but then, the show was only his second most important moment of Paris fashion week . Louis Vuitton is the flagship brand of luxury giant LVMH, which contributes about 1% to French GDP, placing it close to the core of economic and cultural power in Paris.

On Friday Ghesquière, who has led Vuitton for a decade, was knighted by President Emmanuel Macron for his contribution to French creative industries, at a ceremony at the Élysée Palace.

The first lady, Brigitte Macron, has a longstanding close collaboration with Ghesquière, attending his shows and wearing custom looks for state occasions. President Macron began his speech joking that “it feels strange to be decorating someone tonight who is used to looking at my wife from every angle … she just told me you are the second man in her life.”

Guests at the ceremony reflected the broad reach of Louis Vuitton, with Catherine Deneuve and the British designer Phoebe Philo alongside K-pop star Felix of Stray Kids. Ghesquière wore a striking double-breasted Louis Vuitton black suit, with a single button fastening and no lapel. Pinning the red ribboned medallion to his chest, Macron said: “This evening … it is the Republic itself that is adding a new element to your wardrobe.”

items.lbText:
High court finding in favour of Hunter Valley community group sets precedent other environmentalists should follow, advocate says

Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast

A landmark decision in Australia’s first climate change high court case has been described as a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that exported greenhouse gas emissions “cannot simply be ignored”.

On Wednesday morning, the nation’s highest court ruled that the approval of MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine expansion in NSW’s Hunter Valley was invalid, in a judgment that sets a precedent for fossil fuel projects in the state.

The coal company brought the high court case after a local community group, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg), halted the coalmine expansion on climate grounds in the NSW court of appeal.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burnt overseas. Known as scope 3 emissions, these are not counted in Australia’s domestic tally.

Commenting on the judgment, the deputy Greens leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said: “For too long, big coal and gas companies have tried to pretend that the emissions from their products are someone else’s problem once they leave Australian shores. They’re not.

“When Australian coal is burned overseas, the climate damage doesn’t magically disappear at the port. It comes back to communities here through worsening heat, drought, bushfires and floods.

“This judgment sends a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that the climate impacts of their projects cannot simply be ignored or pushed down the line.”

NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson, formerly a public interest environmental lawyer, also said the high court judgment could lead to “significant legal difficulty” for the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension, which was approved by the IPC a week ago.

In greenlighting the HVO extension – the biggest in the state’s history – the IPC ruled that emissions from the mine would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”, but that their impacts had been outweighed by economic benefits to the region.

For both the HVO and Mount Pleasant coal developments, 98% of the emissions were scope 3 emissions, Higginson said. “HVO’s environmental impact statement didn’t even account for scope 3 emissions at all, and the high court has been crystal clear that consent authorities must ensure emissions are minimised to the greatest extent practicable. It seems clear that the approval of HVO fails this test.

“Lawyers should be running to the courts right now with this judgment in hand, ready to stop coal approvals in their tracks,” she said.

In a joint statement, the Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, and the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, described the decision as a threat to “Australia’s standing as a reliable energy exporter” and said the federal and NSW governments “must act immediately to fix the law”.

“A project extension the Independent Planning Commission approved in 2022, after years of assessment, has been sent back to square one,” they said, arguing that the Minns government should amend NSW’s Environmental Planning and Assessment Act to “make clear that overseas emissions from Australia’s exported resources are not a consideration in project approvals”.

The climate change minister, Chris Bowen, who is in Fiji chairing climate negotiations, said: “The law of the land is law of the land, as interpreted by the high court, and we respect that.

“If others don’t, if others are so biased in their approach that they don’t respect the law of the land, that’s a matter for them. It says a bit about their approach, but that’s about as all I’m going to say because it’s a court case and I’m not in Australia at the moment.”

Murray Watt, the federal environment minister, said on Wednesday afternoon that while he had not had an opportunity to review the judgment in full, “the decision from the high court is in relation to a New South Wales government decision based on New South Wales legislation”.

“It doesn’t automatically transfer to commonwealth decisions or commonwealth legislation,” he told News24.

The NSW government was contacted for comment.

items.title: Coalition MPs concede immigration pledge not fully costed by independent watchdog
items.author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
items.content:
Angus Taylor says opposition ‘worked closely’ with Parliamentary Budget Office but Liberal sources say it has not yet conducted a full analysis of the policy

Taylor, and the deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, have said repeatedly the Coalition “worked closely” with the independent budget watchdog on its plan to reduce net overseas migration to 100,000 for two years.

items.lbText:
Angus Taylor says opposition ‘worked closely’ with Parliamentary Budget Office but Liberal sources say it has not yet conducted a full analysis of the policy

Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast

Coalition MPs concede the party’s newly released immigration policy has not been costed in full by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), despite Angus Taylor defending the plan as “budget neutral”.

Taylor, and the deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, have said repeatedly the Coalition “worked closely” with the independent budget watchdog on its plan to reduce net overseas migration to 100,000 for two years.

Announced on Tuesday, the policy would see net overseas migration rates of 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in the fourth.

Business and the university sector have warned the cuts are arbitrary , dangerous for the economy and likely to exacerbate shortages in key sectors, including health and aged care.

Taylor’s office said they planned to have the policy costed before the next federal election, but have used internal analysis and existing costings during the design process. Coalition sources told Guardian Australia the PBO had not conducted a full analysis of the new policy before its release.

PBO officials are not allowed to discuss costings for members of parliament but can choose to clarify references in media reports if they are incorrect or misrepresent PBO work.

The PBO declined to comment on Wednesday.

“We’ve been working closely with the Parliamentary Budget Office on analysis of our initiatives and we are confident that this package is budget neutral,” Taylor said announcing the plan on Tuesday.

He said the Coalition had “done exactly what the government does” and then accused Labor of not releasing modelling.

Labor and One Nation both want to bring down international arrivals, seeking to capitalise on growing anti-migration sentiment and pressure on housing and essential services.

A policy document said the Coalition had worked with the PBO to assess “the impact of the package on the budget”, finding it would generate a small positive return.

Challenged over the release of PBO costings on Wednesday, Taylor told Channel Nine: “We’ve released the outcomes of that budget analysis that we’ve been doing …

“We have released the figures, and we’ve said it’s budget neutral, and we’ve laid that out.”

The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, warned that the Coalition plan would hurt agriculture, aged care and even defence.

“What we see from the Liberal party is actually policy chasing One Nation rather than policy in the national interest,” he said during a visit to Perth.

“Immigration is absolutely central to this. We need to get the numbers right. We do need to manage them down. That’s what our government’s doing, but we need to do it in a way which can maintain our economy and maintain vital sectors like the defence industry here in Western Australia.”

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss, Andrew McKellar, rejected the planned cuts, arguing Australia had a housing supply problem, not an immigration problem.

“When we look at what the Coalition has said, even when we look at what the government and One Nation have said, the problem is each of them are starting from the proposal that they’re targeting a net overseas migration figure. That’s the wrong place to start.”

items.title: Scientists who put faith in technology less likely to take climate action
items.author: Matthew Taylor
items.content:
‘Techno-optimism’ may lead to reliance on unproven solutions at expense of societal changes needed

Scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action on the issue, according to a study.

The report from the London School of Economics found they are 23% less likelyto sign petitions or take part in protests than peers who doubt that technology is the answer. They are also 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, from reducing flights to changing to a vegan or vegetarian diet.

‘Techno-optimism’ may lead to reliance on unproven solutions at expense of societal changes needed

Scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action on the issue, according to a study.

The report from the London School of Economics found they are 23% less likelyto sign petitions or take part in protests than peers who doubt that technology is the answer. They are also 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, from reducing flights to changing to a vegan or vegetarian diet.

Fabian Dablander, the lead author, said the belief that technology will largely solve climate change and its consequences, labelled “techno-optimism”, can lead to an over reliance on unproven solutions at the expense of the far-reaching socioeconomic transformations needed to address the climate and nature crisis.

“Technological solutions are often politically attractive because they promise to address climate change without requiring changes to how people live and consume,” said Dablander.

“Strikingly, we see the same tendency at the individual level, with greater faith in technological solutions going hand in hand with less engagement in climate action. Yet technology cannot substitute for the broader societal changes and large-scale shifts in consumption that are also needed.”

The study surveyed more than 9,000 scientists across 115 countries. Overall 27% said they agreed with the statement “technology will largely solve the problems caused by climate change” and 44% disagreed (29% neither agreed nor disagreed).

The “techno-optimist” scientists reported engaging in less civic actions and protests, signed fewer petitions and engaged in less advocacy. They were also less likely to reduce the number of flights they took, cut their car usage or follow a mostly vegan or vegetarian diet .

The report, published in Environmental Research Letters, also found that techno-optimism was most prevalent among scientists with right leaning political views and those working in applied and natural sciences.

Prof Kevin Anderson, one of the world’s leading climate scientists, of the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research at the University of Manchester, who was not involved in the study, said in his experience “a significant proportion of climate academics who enjoy very high incomes from their work, particularly when those incomes are accompanied by prestige, status and glittering honours, have enthusiastically swallowed the blue pill”.

“It offers a convenient escape from any uncomfortable sense of personal responsibility, allowing them to maintain the comforting fiction that they are deeply concerned about the world their children will inherit while continuing to live lives that contribute disproportionately to the problem.”

He added the “accompanying faith in future technological salvation provides another crutch: a way of postponing difficult choices today by placing hope in solutions that may arrive tomorrow”.

“Yet strikingly often, the evidential basis for these promises falls far short of the standards of scrutiny they would demand of research conducted by others. The result is a remarkable inversion of scientific practice: the more uncomfortable the implications of the evidence, the greater the enthusiasm for believing in a future that the evidence does not support.”

items.lbText:
Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Sydney in February 2024

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

A detective has broken down in court while describing the moment she found the bodies of two men allegedly murdered by former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon.

Jesse Baird, 26, and his new boyfriend Luke Davies, 29, were shot dead in a Sydney terrace in February 2024.

Lamarre-Condon, Baird’s ex and a then-police officer, has pleaded not guilty to murder, arguing the men died in two separate violent struggles after he entered the home disguised as a food delivery rider.

His subsequent efforts to dispose of their bodies at Bungonia – 200km south of Sydney – were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths, his lawyer has said.

A detective who co-ordinated a search of Cella Farm, where Lamarre-Condon allegedly tried unsuccessfully to sink the bodies in a dam, told the alleged murderer’s trial how she eventually found the remains of the two slain men eight days after the shooting.

Detective Senior Constable Christine Abela had been involved in searching the farm, where crime scene officers discovered a padlock had been cut, the jury heard.

Prosecutors allege the lock was cut with an angle grinder Lamarre-Condon had asked his friend to buy on the drive from Sydney.

Concrete blocks and gym weights were found at the edge of a dam on the farm, the jury was told.

On 27 February, Abela was diverted to a Greek monastery about 20km away.

“There was a strong smell as soon as I got out of the car,” she told a NSW supreme court jury on Wednesday.

The detective became emotional as prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC took her through her memories of the odour becoming stronger as she approached two blue and silver surfboard bags.

The bags were covered with sticks, branches and stones, the detective said.

The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon became infatuated with Baird after they broke off contact in November 2023, resolving to murder him.

However, Lamarre-Condon’s close friend Nicole Harvell told the court on Wednesday she could not remember any conversation with the ex-officer about Baird after the pair broke up for the final time.

That was despite her being in almost daily contact with the now-31-year-old.

Senior Constable Harvell recalled trying to contact her friend when she saw media reports that he was under suspicion for the two men’s deaths.

“Fuck Beau, are you ok?” she texted to Lamarre-Condon’s phone.

The sworn officer maintained under cross-examination the accused killer had months earlier told her about enlisting his mother to help him lie to Baird.

Lamarre-Condon posted an Instagram story with a bunch of flowers and the caption: “When he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these.”

But publication was restricted to select friends that did not include Baird.

The photo was designed to imply Baird sent flowers to the accused, despite the pair not being in a relationship at the time, Harvell said.

When Baird discovered the ruse, Lamarre-Condon spent $160 on a bouquet identical to the photo to lie to Baird, the officer’s friend said.

Lamarre-Condon then sent a photo to Baird showing his mother with the fresh bouquet.

The bouquet had a handwritten note to imply his mother had been the intended recipient and they were from her partner, who was in Melbourne, the jury heard.

“I recall the accused telling me his mother had written that note,” Harvell said.

items.lbText:
Uneeb Ullah, 28, from Ipswich, has been remanded in custody after his arrest on Tuesday evening for the alleged murder of the child

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

A Queensland man has been charged with the murder of his three-month-old baby son, after the boy died in hospital this week.

The infant, from the Ipswich area west of Brisbane, died almost a week after being taken to hospital with “significant internal injuries”. The boy had been on life support.

Uneeb Ullah, 28, was arrested on Tuesday evening and charged with the boy’s murder, which is designated a domestic violence offence.

His matter was mentioned briefly in court on Wednesday but Ullah was not required to appear and did not enter a plea.

Police said detectives from the Child Protection Investigation Unit launched an investigation on 1 October after the boy was taken to Ipswich hospital with significant injuries, and that the nature of those injuries prompted hospital staff to report the matter to police.

He was later transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, DI Michael Manago said the mother of the child was “extremely upset” and that both parents, who were born overseas, have limited support.

“This is a terribly tragic event involving a very vulnerable young member of the community,” Det Insp. Manago said.

“The boy’s mother is extremely upset as you can imagine; this is a terribly tragic event.

“She is struggling, but we’re offering her all the support that we can through this very difficult time.”

Police said they had spoken to the couple several times since they opened the investigation. The investigation would include looking at the “nature and dynamics” of the boy’s parents’ relationship.

“It’s an incredibly confronting and difficult investigation,” Manago said.

“We were conducting our investigation throughout the last number of days and gathering evidence.

When Ullah’s case came before the court on Wednesday, police prosecutor Ben Messina asked it be stood down until later in the day.

“I received a phone call this morning … that potentially more material would be provided and asked [that] this matter be stood down to the end of the list,” Messina said of the “relatively vague request”.

The magistrate agreed to re-mention the case if other charges were laid.

Kirstyn Nicholson, a Legal Aid solicitor representing Ullah, did not apply for bail and sought an adjournment.

Ullah was remanded in custody until the matter returns to court on 26 October.

This story was amended on 7 October 2026. A previous version incorrectly stated Uneeb Ullah was from Logan

items.lbText:
Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in Melbourne

New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, 29, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.

Hammami, an Omani national, had allegedly used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air, the United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said. Israeli and other officials in the region suspect he originally planned for such an attack in July , but postponed it.

The New Zealand police assistant commissioner, Michael Johnson, on Tuesday confirmed the man was in the country on a student visa for 175 days, from 30 November 2018 to 23 May 2019.

“Police can confirm the co-pilot was in New Zealand to complete a portion of his flight training for a UK-based company, no longer operating in New Zealand,” Johnson said in a statement

The police are now investigating his time in the country, Johnson said.

New Zealand joins multiple countries scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted alone.

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree , RMIT University in Melbourne confirmed.

On a now deleted social media profile believed to belong to Hammami, the then student appears in a selfie with other teenagers in a shopping centre food court in Melbourne’s CBD.

The UK’s Telegraph reported on a post on a now deleted X account that appears to be linked to Hammami that described his years studying overseas as “the golden years of my religious commitment”, and claimed he became less observant when he returned to Oman.

On Wednesday, Australia’s peak Jewish body, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, called for a thorough investigation of Hammami’s associations in the country.

“We have seen over the years the availability of extremist literature in religious bookstores, the presence of preachers of hate and violence and the capacity for those living in Australia to fall under the sway of recruiters and nefarious street preachers,” the council’s co-chief executive, Alex Ryvchin, said in a statement.

“We have to understand who associated with this [alleged] terrorist, who influenced him and what vestiges of his murderous ideology remain.”

The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar , who also trained in New Zealand for a time, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.

In a phone call on Saturday with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

items.title: Tories delight as satirical tapestry pokes fun at ‘turncoat’ Robert Jenrick
items.author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent

Robert Jenrick, bested by Badenoch in the leadership contest a year earlier, looked on, and – as one shadow cabinet member now recalls – had to be prodded by Lord Ashcroft to applaud. “If you’re plotting against someone, then you at least pretend to like them,” they say. “The thing about Robert is he’s not even a good machiavellian.”

items.lbText:
Reminders of banished Reform UK defector were all around the Conservative party conference in Birmingham

As Kemi Badenoch basked in the applause of the Tory faithful at the close of her pivotal speech at Conservative party conference last year, one member of her shadow cabinet looked less than enthused.

Robert Jenrick, bested by Badenoch in the leadership contest a year earlier, looked on, and – as one shadow cabinet member now recalls – had to be prodded by Lord Ashcroft to applaud. “If you’re plotting against someone, then you at least pretend to like them,” they say. “The thing about Robert is he’s not even a good machiavellian.”

Jenrick left the party a matter of months later, swiftly – and publicly – ejected by an ice-cold Badenoch after she got wind that he was planning to defect to Reform. This week, as the Conservative ranks enjoy their annual knees-up in Birmingham, the now Reform UK economy spokesperson has been swiping from the sidelines, accusing his old party of “once again copying our policies”.

But while Jenrick’s physical presence may be absent from the migraine-inducing interior of the International Convention Centre in the West Midlands, members could be forgiven for sighing that everywhere they looked, something reminded them of him.

At the heart of the conference, members queue to chortle at depictions of Jenrick in the Conservatives’ own “Birmingham tapestry”, a 27-metre (88ft) woven graphical retelling of the past two years in British politics, as seen through Conservative eyes.

Featuring Badenoch as a glorious 11th-century conquering warrior, the “tapestry” also depicts a tiny Jenrick wailing as he loses the leadership contest, as he watches a crowd cheering on his victor. A little later, under the heading “Expelleth the Turncoat”, an outsized Badenoch is seen banishing her tiny, sobbing former colleague – as she stands next to a photocopier where, legend has it, Jenrick’s resignation letter was found.

“I think it’s great fun; every story needs a villain and he’s ours,” says one party member who’d travelled from Scotland for the event. “He’s not a big figure here any more, he’s just a figure of fun.”

Another member says they voted for Jenrick in the leadership election and had felt let down by his plots to remove the leader after failing to get the top job. “The way he did what he did was spiteful, petty and childish. I was a massive fan, but now I couldn’t care less what he does,” he says. Referring to Jenrick’s hyperactive social media output, which regularly show the Reform economy spokesperson confronting fare-dodgers and shoplifters, he rolls his eyes. “It’s just attention-seeking, isn’t it?” he says. “I do wonder now, though, as Reform falter, if he regrets what he did. I hope so.”

The schadenfreude at Jenrick’s fading star is palpable at this conference. Unprompted, shadow cabinet ministers bring him up with unbridled delight. “I miss him like I would miss an abscess in my molar,” remarks one senior Tory, before wondering aloud about whether Jenrick was likely to be punched in the face during one of his vigilante operations.

Others are surprised at their own strength of feeling towards a former colleague. “Nobody knew how much we hated Robert until he left the party,” says one senior member. Repeating the mantra that they are more united behind Badenoch than any other leader in years, some credit Jenrick for bringing them closer together, because he had “briefed against everybody”. Another adds: “Rob leaving was like pulling out a splinter.”

The commentary is not limited to gossip around the bars of Birmingham’s Hyatt hotel. Mentions of Jenrick are met with groans in the audience at a packed fringe event of shadow cabinet ministers hosted by More in Common. Asked if he would consider taking Jenrick or any of the other three Tory MPs who defected back, the response of Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, is unequivocal. “No, no, no and no,” he says. Was he relieved they were gone? “Yes, yes, yes and yes.”

Badenoch has made clear that neither Jenrick nor his fellow defectors (variously described by her team as “venal”, “mad” and “hopeless”) would ever be welcome back, going as far as thanking Nigel Farage for doing the “spring cleaning” of her party for her.

Others suggest Reform were welcome to one of their former star players. “Good luck to his new friends in Reform,” one says. “It’s all about Rob and his own ambitions and he’d elbow them into the path of an oncoming express train if it meant he got ahead.”

Appreciating the Birmingham tapestry in between panel sessions, the shadow undersecretary for environment, food and rural affairs, Aphra Brandreth, insists the party is completely over Jenrick, although his shadow here suggests there may still be some healing left to do. “Honestly I don’t spend any time thinking about Robert Jenrick,” she says, with a benevolent smile. “He’s gone, and we’ve all moved on.”

items.lbText:
Christopher Alan Saunders becomes highest-ranked Catholic in Australia convicted of sexual abuse over his time as member of clergy

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

A former high-ranking Catholic known for hosting boozy parties will spend at least four and a half years behind bars for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men.

The ex-bishop of Broome Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, was found guilty of 13 sex offences after a jury trial in the West Australian district court.

The offending between 2008 and 2019 included one count of sexual penetration without consent and a dozen unlawful and indecent assault charges.

Saunders was sentenced on Wednesday to six years and six months’ imprisonment.

He will be eligible for parole after serving four years and six months.

Unless acquitted on appeal, the long-serving bishop would be the highest-ranking Catholic in Australia convicted of sexual abuse over his time as a member of the clergy.

The late Cardinal George Pell was found guilty in 2018 but later acquitted by the high court of raping one choirboy and molesting another in 1996.

Saunders was acquitted by the jury of six other charges, including two counts of indecently dealing with a child over 16 under his authority and four counts of unlawful and indecent assault.

He was acquitted of a further seven similar charges during the trial due to the lack of evidence.

The sentence was backdated to August when Saunders was convicted and taken into custody.

Prosecutors said Saunders, known as Brother B by his victims, put on alcohol-fuelled parties at Catholic church-owned properties to get access to Aboriginal boys and men so he could sexually assault them.

“The accused had a sexual interest in young Aboriginal men and a tendency to act on that interest when the opportunity presented itself,” the prosecutor, Adam Ebell, previously told the court.

Saunders was ordained as the second Broome bishop in 1996 and presided over 13 schools and nine parishes before stepping aside in 2020 when the sex abuse claims became public.

Pope Francis accepted his resignation a year later.

A church probe into the retired clergyman’s activities was suspended when the West Australian police started investigating him.

It will restart now the trial has finished.

“Its findings will inform decisions in Rome about Christopher Saunders’ position in the church,” archbishop Timothy Costelloe said in August.

Costelloe said the jury’s guilty verdict concerned crimes “that violate the dignity and betray the trust of victims and survivors”.

“The victims, survivors and other witnesses who came forward showed great courage and resilience throughout a long and difficult process,” he said.

Russian officials said a Liberian-flagged tanker was attacked and a crew of 23 Indian nationals rescued

An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said.

The transport ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked and that “crude oil is burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”.

“Firefighting efforts will begin once the fire’s intensity has subsided and rescue vessels can safely approach the tanker,” the ministry said.

A crew of 23 – all Indian citizens – had been rescued, it added.

Russia and Ukraine have targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since the conflict began, and Russia has recently attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.

There was no comment from Kyiv on the attack.

Videos and photos circulated on social media from Sochi – a popular Black Sea resort city of almost 500,000 people – showed bright orange flames out at sea and a thick column of black smoke billowing into the sky.

Local officials restricted access to the coast and beaches.

Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bulgaria’s prime minister said that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones in the first attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.

Bulgarian authorities said that the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the drone strikes. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev condemned the attack.

After an emergency government meeting, Radev said: “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.” Radev said after an emergency government meeting.

Sea and aerial drones attacked the ships about 80 miles (128km) off Bulgaria’s coast, he said.

Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address on Tuesday that a “massive strike” from Russia was likely to come, and in the early hours of Wednesday Kyiv was attacked.

Russian strikes damaged buildings and warehouses across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor ​Vitali ‌Klitschko said ‌on Telegram.

Agence France-Presse reported multiple explosions in Kyiv, and Reuters reported two people were killed by Russian strikes.

A separate Russian strike on Ukraine’s south-eastern city of Dnipro damaged ⁠an industrial facility, ​officials said, without giving details.

Kyiv has been under increased attack as winter approaches, with Russian airstrikes targeting energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro river. Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly day and night, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.

items.lbText:
Mood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese imports

EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars into Europe .

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday.

Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, where China is high on the agenda.

The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months.

Diplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024 there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars , which were not subject to tariffs.

Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted.

It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries.

On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice.

In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”.

The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”.

Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”.

Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.”

Sources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called “trade bazooka” available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used.

Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement.

Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”.

“Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.

items.lbText:
Owens sued over September Instagram post that suggested trio tampered with evidence in death of Mississippi teen

Three friends of Nolan Wells , a Mississippi teen who died after a July boating trip, have sued NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation.

On 26 September, Owens shared an Instagram video that suggested Wells’s friends Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour had deleted evidence from Wells’s phone after his death, which the three men denied in their lawsuit.

“Arrest them immediately!! Like yesterday,” Owens captioned the post.

In a Monday complaint filed in a Mississippi district court, the fathers of the three young men, who are also named in the complaint as plaintiffs because they are deemed minors under state law, accuse Owens of harming their reputation and endangering their physical safety with the post.

“Due to the conduct of Owens and many other less-famous individuals, these completely innocent young men have been subjected to thousands of death threats, face-to-face harassment, and daily fear and ridicule from complete strangers. They’ve even been refused service at public establishments. Their lives, and the lives of their family members, will never be the same,” the complaint alleges.

Owens could not be immediately reached for comment.

The friends’ counsel also indicated they intend to take legal action against other public figures who have been vocal about Wells’s death including Al Sharpton and The View’s Sunny Hostin.

On 4 July, Wells and his friends sailed for a Mississippi island. He was last seen that afternoon. Two days later, his body was found on the island.

The circumstances of his death have fueled public suspicion. Wells, who was African American, had been partying with a mostly white friend group – a detail that gained traction online as some referenced Mississippi’s past with racial violence.

In late September, a Mississippi grand jury declined to file criminal charges, finding Wells’s death to appear “consistent with drowning”. Jackson county district attorney Angel Myers McIlrath has said Wells’s death was not racially motivated.

Wells’s parents and civil rights lawyer Ben Crump continue to call for further investigations, citing the state’s autopsy report, which said Wells’s airways and stomach were empty. His family has said the lack of water found undermines the drowning determination.

“I cannot take that ruling, and I cannot move on with my life,” Christine Wonsley, Wells’s mother, reportedly said , referring to the grand jury’s findings at a Monday press conference. “We have been left with more questions and heartbreak than any answers.”

Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs

Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine , pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.

Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans , saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.

Collins’ defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.

Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.

Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.

“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.

“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”

Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democrat presidential candidates in every election since 1992.

Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”.

Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine.

“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”

Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border.

“I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.”

Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

Ellison admits ‘good relationship’ with administration in remarks to reporters about newly merged media company

David Ellison, the chief executive of the newly formed media conglomerate Skydance, denied that he has “politicized” the company despite the close connection he has forged with Donald Trump’s White House over the 20 months of his administration.

“We have a good relationship with this administration,” Ellison acknowledged to reporters at a Tuesday press briefing focused on the now-consummated merger of Paramount Skydance and CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery.

“I also had a really good relationship with President Biden. I have a good relationship with [Republican South Carolina senator] Tim Scott, and I have a good relationship with Governor Gavin Newsom. I think it is important to talk to everybody on both sides of the aisle … When you’re operating within a business-friendly administration, you should always have those relationships.”

“We want to speak to everybody,” Ellison added. “We do not want to politicize the company.”

Asked about his conversations with Trump about CNN, Ellison did not directly discuss his communications with the president, the network’s most prominent critic. But he said he wanted to clarify that “we have not talked to any political leader of any party about news, other than to say that we want to be in the truth business and we want to be in the trust business. And we believe in complete editorial independence.”

Amid concerns about whether Ellison might move CNN in a more rightward editorial direction, he said that both the cable news network and CBS News would be “completely editorially independent”, echoing a message he delivered earlier in the day during a town hall meeting with company employees.

Ellison also gave an endorsement to the two leaders he has tapped to continue running the two news networks networks he now controls, CNN chief executive Mark Thompson and CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss.

On Monday, Thompson told staffers in a memo that he would remain at the merged company, while Skydance also confirmed that Weiss would remain in her role.

“We’re thrilled, obviously, with Mark,” Ellison said. “We’re thrilled with Bari.”

Asked about a potential merging of CBS News and CNN and any cuts – or “synergies” – that might stem from that, Ellison said he and his leadership team would spend the next several months “basically getting under the hood on all of that”. Most of the $6bn in expected savings from the merger would not come from job losses, he said.

Ellison was not asked about Weiss’s performance as the editorial leader of CBS News. When asked specifically about Weiss’s performance by a Guardian reporter in June, Ellison ignored the question.

As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases

Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher.

Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town.

For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers.

“I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.”

In southern California , Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”.

Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025.

During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee.

“Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking only on behalf of himself.)

“It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.”

Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US. “His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.” The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego.

“This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.”

Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke.

“I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X . “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran.

“The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”

Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones

New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed.

Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities.

“The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian.

New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said.

“Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said.

The report finds that as the climate heats, glaciers are shrinking . New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said.

Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume.

“We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said.

Greenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever.

“That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said.

Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress.

Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans were warming 34% faster than the global average which has been linked to mass sea sponge bleaching , die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scale fish standings and penguin deaths .

The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment.

The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places.

Severe storms, including Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods in 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs.

New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said.

“Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”

Justice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspect

A surprise suspected accomplice has been arrested in connection with a mass school shooting in Canada that was made notorious after an 18-year-old allegedly killed six children after discussing it with the AI chatbot ChatGPT.

The US Department of Justice said Tuesday it had detained James Codey Bryant, 30, a resident of western Washington state, on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Bryant offered money and “technical advice” to the suspected shooter for six months leading up to the killings, the justice department alleged.

Canadian police have identified the suspect in this year’s massacre of eight people – including her mother and half-brother, as well as the six children, making it the second-deadliest school shooting in the country’s history – as Jesse Van Rootselaar, who has a history of mental health problems.

It had been known that Van Rootselaar had used ChatGPT to plan the attack, which took place in February. The safety team at OpenAI, the company that owns the chatbot, flagged Van Rootselaar internally after she conducted conversations with it about gun violence, but the company did not alert police. It did reportedly close Van Rootselaar’s account, but she started a second one that was not closed. Victims’ families and the province of British Columbia have sued OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, for failing to report her behaviour.

It was not previously known publicly that Van Rootselaar was also talking to a human about her plans.

In a joint press conference with the justice department and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) on Tuesday, authorities alleged that Bryant and Van Rootselaar met on the now-defunct messaging service Omegle about three years prior to the shooting and kept in contact.

Neil Floyd, acting US attorney, and W Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge for the FBI’s Seattle bureau, said they believe Bryant sent Van Rootselaar about $100 to buy new shoes and aabout $15 for a lighter.

Authorities said there is no indication so far that the two suspects ever met in person.

According to an indictment obtained by CBC , Bryant was “knowingly and wilfully” conspiring with Van Rootselaar beginning in or before August 2025.

That August, Bryant told Van Rootselaar the pair should “find a way to delete” their messages, and in mid-December Bryant suggested getting a VPN to avoid detection for “posting a shooting video online”, according to the court document reviewed by CBC.

Police said that on several occasions Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing the attack, but did not contact law enforcement.

They added that after Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother and brother in their family home, she was unable to start the car. Bryant advised her on how to turn on the engine, thereby allowing the shooter to reach the school and execute the attack, authorities said.

Bryant also allegedly agreed to livestream the mass shooting, which Harrington said police were not sure Van Rootselaar would have committed had Bryant not done so.

It was not clear whether the suspect was represented by a lawyer. Bryant will be prosecuted in the US as a US citizen under an investigation by the FBI, which said it will continue working closely with Canadian authorities.
